title: What is Delta Lake — an open-source storage layer on top of Parquet that brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and DML (UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE) to a data lake — and how does it differ from plain Parquet (transaction log, concurrent writes, schema evolution)?
shortTitle: What is Delta Lake and how it differs from plain Parquet

s1_definition.profdef: Delta Lake is an open-source storage layer that sits on top of Parquet files and adds a transaction log (the `_delta_log` directory) to turn a plain folder of files into a fully transactional table. It gives you ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel to older versions, and row-level DML operations such as UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE, none of which plain Parquet supports. The transaction log is an ordered record of every commit, and readers reconstruct the current table state by replaying it, which is what makes concurrent reads and writes safe.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps all its transaction records as plain Parquet files in a folder. If Rajesh's transfer writes new files while a report is being generated, the report might read half-written data — there is no referee. Delta Lake adds a strict ledger (the transaction log) that records "at version 5, these files are the truth." Everyone reads the ledger first, so nobody ever sees a half-finished write, and you can even ask "show me the table as it was at version 3 this morning."
s1_definition.oneliner: Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log that turns a dumb folder of files into an ACID, versioned, updatable table.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Delta Lake is an open-source storage layer that sits on top of Parquet files and adds a transaction log (the `_delta_log` directory) to turn a plain folder of files into a fully transactional table. It gives you ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel to older versions, and row-level DML operations such as UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE, none of which plain Parquet supports. The transaction log is an ordered record of every commit, and readers reconstruct the current table state by replaying it, which is what makes concurrent reads and writes safe.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps all its transaction records as plain Parquet files in a folder. If Rajesh's transfer writes new files while a report is being generated, the report might read half-written data — there is no referee. Delta Lake adds a strict ledger (the transaction log) that records "at version 5, these files are the truth." Everyone reads the ledger first, so nobody ever sees a half-finished write, and you can even ask "show me the table as it was at version 3 this morning."

**One line to remember:** Delta Lake is Parquet plus a transaction log that turns a dumb folder of files into an ACID, versioned, updatable table.

sections.s2_technical:
Plain Parquet is just a columnar file format. A "Parquet table" is really a directory of `.parquet` files with no coordinator. When a writer adds or rewrites files, a concurrent reader can see a partial result, there is no way to atomically replace data, and there is no history. Delta Lake fixes all of this by adding the `_delta_log` folder containing JSON commit files (`00000000000000000000.json`, `...0001.json`, and so on) plus periodic Parquet checkpoints.

Each commit in the log is an atomic set of actions such as `add` (a new data file is now part of the table), `remove` (a file is logically deleted), and `metaData` (schema or partitioning changed). To read the table at version N, Delta replays commits 0 through N and computes the set of currently valid files. Because the commit itself is a single atomic file creation, either the whole change is visible or none of it is, which is the Atomicity and Isolation of ACID.

Concurrency uses optimistic concurrency control. Two writers can both prepare commits; when they try to write the next log entry, the file name is `...0007.json`, and only one can create that file first. The loser detects the conflict, re-reads the latest state, and retries. In code you simply call `df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(path)` and Delta handles the protocol.

Schema enforcement means Delta rejects a write whose columns or types do not match the table, protecting you from silently corrupting data. For example `df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(path)` throws if `df` has a column that is not in the table. Schema evolution is opt-in with `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`, which safely adds new columns. DML is first-class: `DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).delete("status = 'CANCELLED'")` physically rewrites only the affected files and records the change in the log, something impossible on raw Parquet without rewriting the whole dataset yourself.

A senior nuance is that Delta does not mutate Parquet files in place; UPDATE and DELETE rewrite the files that contain matching rows and record the swap in the log, so reads are always consistent and old files remain for time travel until `VACUUM` removes them.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores its daily `transactions` dataset as Parquet files in a data lake. Every night a batch job appends the day's transfers, and at the same time analysts run reports. One morning a report showed a total that did not match the ledger because it read a half-written set of files. This is exactly what Delta Lake's transaction log prevents: readers only ever see committed versions, so a report either sees yesterday's complete data or today's complete data, never a mix.

Problem 2 — A compliance officer asked "what did this table look like at 2 AM before the correction job ran?" With plain Parquet there is no answer because old files may be overwritten. This is exactly what Delta's versioned log gives us: every append creates a new version, and we can read any past version.

Problem 3 — A bad upstream feed once added an extra column and corrupted the dataset. Delta's schema enforcement would have rejected that write outright. This maps to the schema-enforcement feature.

What the code will do: a Python PySpark demo (`DeltaBankingDemo`) that creates a Delta table of transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), appends a new transaction, inspects the transaction log, performs a DELETE to cancel a transaction, and shows that the table history records every version.

##### 4b. SQL / Delta DDL Script

```sql
-- Delta table created via Spark SQL (metadata lives in _delta_log, not a traditional DB)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS transactions (
    txn_id      STRING,
    account_id  STRING,
    amount      DECIMAL(15,2),
    txn_type    STRING,
    status      STRING,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP
) USING DELTA
LOCATION '/data/warehouse/transactions';

-- Seed rows for Rajesh and Priya
INSERT INTO transactions VALUES
 ('TXN-1','SAV2001', 50000.00,'TRANSFER','COMPLETED', current_timestamp()),
 ('TXN-2','CUR3001', 25000.00,'DEPOSIT' ,'COMPLETED', current_timestamp());
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```text
# conf/spark-defaults.conf
spark.sql.extensions            io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension
spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog
spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled true
```
sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/delta_banking_demo.py
# Runnable PySpark + Delta Lake demo for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("DeltaBankingDemo")

PATH = "/data/warehouse/transactions"

def build_spark() -> SparkSession:
    # configure Delta extensions on the SparkSession
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("DeltaBankingDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                    "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
            .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def create_table(spark: SparkSession) -> None:
    rows = [("TXN-1", "SAV2001", Decimal("50000.00"), "TRANSFER", "COMPLETED"),
            ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", Decimal("25000.00"), "DEPOSIT",  "COMPLETED")]
    df = (spark.createDataFrame(rows,
            ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount", "txn_type", "status"])
            .withColumn("created_at", F.current_timestamp()))
    # overwrite to create a clean version 0
    df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(PATH)
    log.info("Created Delta table at version 0 with %d rows", df.count())

def append_txn(spark: SparkSession) -> None:
    new = (spark.createDataFrame(
            [("TXN-3", "SAV2001", Decimal("12000.00"), "TRANSFER", "COMPLETED")],
            ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount", "txn_type", "status"])
            .withColumn("created_at", F.current_timestamp()))
    # schema enforcement runs here: columns/types must match or it throws
    new.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(PATH)
    log.info("Appended TXN-3 -> new table version created in _delta_log")

def cancel_txn(spark: SparkSession) -> None:
    dt = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, PATH)
    # row-level DELETE: rewrites only affected files, records a remove+add commit
    dt.delete("txn_id = 'TXN-2'")
    log.info("Deleted TXN-2 via Delta DML (impossible on plain Parquet)")

def show_history(spark: SparkSession) -> None:
    hist = (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, PATH).history()
            .select("version", "timestamp", "operation"))
    log.info("Delta table history (each row = one committed version):")
    hist.show(truncate=False)

def main() -> None:
    spark = build_spark()
    create_table(spark)
    append_txn(spark)
    cancel_txn(spark)
    show_history(spark)
    log.info("Current table state:")
    spark.read.format("delta").load(PATH).orderBy("txn_id").show(truncate=False)
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/delta_io/table_writer.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame

class TableWriter:
    """Encapsulates safe Delta writes with schema enforcement."""
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def append(self, df: DataFrame) -> None:
        # mergeSchema is deliberately NOT set: strict enforcement by default
        df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(self.path)

    def append_evolving(self, df: DataFrame) -> None:
        # explicit opt-in to schema evolution for new columns
        (df.write.format("delta").option("mergeSchema", "true")
           .mode("append").save(self.path))
```

```python
# File: src/delta_io/table_reader.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame

class TableReader:
    """Reads current or historical versions of a Delta table."""
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession, path: str):
        self.spark = spark
        self.path = path

    def current(self) -> DataFrame:
        return self.spark.read.format("delta").load(self.path)

    def at_version(self, version: int) -> DataFrame:
        return (self.spark.read.format("delta")
                .option("versionAsOf", version).load(self.path))
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two seed transactions (TXN-1 for Rajesh, TXN-2 for Priya), then an appended TXN-3, then a delete of TXN-2.

Step 1: `create_table` writes two Parquet data files and commit `...0000.json` to `_delta_log`. The log's `add` actions point to those two files. The table is now at version 0.

Step 2: A reader calling `spark.read.format("delta").load(PATH)` first reads `_delta_log`, computes the valid file set (the two files), and returns exactly those rows. It never scans half-written files.

Step 3: `append_txn` runs schema enforcement on TXN-3, confirms the columns match, writes one new Parquet file, and commits `...0001.json` with an `add` action. Version becomes 1. The old files are untouched.

Step 4: `cancel_txn` issues a DELETE for TXN-2. Delta finds the file containing TXN-2, writes a new file without that row, and commits `...0002.json` with a `remove` for the old file and an `add` for the new one. Version becomes 2.

Step 5: `show_history` replays the log and reports three versions with their operations. A time-travel read at version 0 would still show TXN-2 because its old file has not been vacuumed.

Final output:

```text

2026-10-30 06:30:03 INFO Appended TXN-3 -> new table version created in _delta_log
2026-10-30 06:30:05 INFO Deleted TXN-2 via Delta DML (impossible on plain Parquet)

|version|timestamp              |operation|
+-------+-----------------------+---------+
|2      |2026-10-30 06:30:05... |DELETE   |
|1      |2026-10-30 06:30:03... |WRITE    |
|0      |2026-10-30 06:30:01... |WRITE    |

|txn_id|account_id|amount  |txn_type|status   |
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Writer: append TXN-3
    │
    ▼
  Delta protocol (optimistic concurrency)
    │ read latest log version = 0
    │ write parquet data file (part-xxxx.snappy.parquet)
    │ attempt commit _delta_log/...0001.json  ── wins the race ──▶ version 1
    ▼
  _delta_log/
    ├─ ...0000.json  (add: file A, file B)   version 0
    ├─ ...0001.json  (add: file C)           version 1
    └─ ...0002.json  (remove: B, add: D)     version 2  ← DELETE TXN-2
    │
    ▼
  Reader: spark.read.format("delta")
    │ replay log 0..2 → valid files = {A, C, D}
    ▼
  Result: {TXN-1, TXN-3}   (TXN-2 removed, consistent snapshot)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Delta Lake is an open-source storage layer that sits on top of Parquet files and adds a transaction log, which lives in a `_delta_log` directory of ordered JSON commits plus periodic checkpoints. That log is what upgrades a plain folder of Parquet files into a real table with ACID guarantees. Plain Parquet is only a file format with no coordinator, so concurrent writes can be seen half-finished, there is no way to atomically replace data, and there is no history. Delta solves all three because every change is committed as one atomic log entry, and readers always reconstruct a consistent snapshot by replaying the log.

Concretely, Delta gives me four things Parquet cannot. It gives ACID transactions through optimistic concurrency control, where two writers race to create the next numbered log file and only one wins while the other retries. It gives schema enforcement, so a write with the wrong columns or types is rejected rather than silently corrupting the table, with schema evolution available as an explicit opt-in through the mergeSchema option. It gives time travel, because every commit is a new version I can read with versionAsOf or timestampAsOf. And it gives row-level DML — UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE — which rewrite only the affected files and record the swap in the log.

At the National Bank of India this mattered directly. Our nightly job appended the day's transactions to a Delta table while analysts ran reports, and because readers only ever see committed versions, a report never again picked up half-written files the way it once had with raw Parquet. When a compliance officer asked what a table looked like before a correction job, I answered with a time-travel read instead of a shrug. And when a bad upstream feed tried to add an unexpected column, schema enforcement rejected it at the door. The way I summarize it in interviews is that Delta is Parquet plus a transaction log, and that log is the difference between a dumb pile of files and a trustworthy, versioned, updatable banking table.
